(Surah al-Kawthar)
Three verses, Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar.﴾

Know that this surah, despite its brevity, contains subtle points (lata'if):

The first: this surah is like a counterpart to the preceding surah, because in the preceding surah Allah, exalted is He, described the hypocrite with four qualities:

The first is stinginess, which is meant by His words: ﴿Who repulses the orphan﴾ ﴿and does not encourage the feeding of the poor﴾ [al-Ma'un: 2-3].

The second is abandoning the prayer, which is meant by His words: ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 5].

The third is showing off in the prayer, which is meant by His words: ﴿who make show [of their deeds]﴾ [al-Ma'un: 6].

The fourth is withholding zakat (obligatory almsgiving), which is meant by His words: ﴿and withhold [even] small kindnesses﴾ [al-Ma'un: 7]. So in this surah, in opposition to those four qualities, He mentions four qualities. Opposite stinginess He says: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, meaning: Indeed, We have given you abundance, so you too give abundantly and do not be stingy. Opposite ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 5] He says: (so pray), meaning: persist in prayer. Opposite ﴿who make show﴾ He says: (to your Lord), meaning: perform the prayer for the pleasure of your Lord, not to be seen by people. Opposite ﴿and withhold [even] small kindnesses﴾ He says: (and sacrifice), and by this He means giving in charity the meat of the sacrificial animals. So consider this wonderful correspondence. Then He concluded the surah with His words: ﴿Indeed, your hater is the one cut off﴾, meaning: the hypocrite who commits those ugly deeds mentioned in that surah will die and no trace or report of his worldly life will remain, whereas as for you, there will remain for you in this world the good remembrance, and in the Hereafter the great reward.

The second point concerning the subtle meanings of this surah: those who travel toward Allah, exalted is He, have three levels. The highest of them is that they be absorbed with their hearts and spirits in the light of the majesty of Allah.

[Page 111]

The second is that they be occupied with acts of worship and bodily devotions.

The third is that they be in the station of restraining the soul from inclining toward sensual pleasures and immediate desires. So His words: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ are an indication of the first station, which is that his holy spirit is distinguished from all other human spirits in quantity and quality. As for quantity, it is because it has more premises; as for quality, it is because it moves from those premises to conclusions more swiftly than other spirits. As for His words: ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾, they are an indication of the second level, and His words: (and sacrifice) are an indication of the third level, since restraining the soul from immediate pleasures is like the slaughtering and sacrificing. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, your hater is the one cut off﴾, and its meaning is that the soul which calls you to seek these sensible things and immediate desires is transient and perishing, whereas "the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord" [al-Kahf: 46], and these are the spiritual felicities and the divine knowledge which are everlasting and eternal. Now let us begin the tafsir (exegesis).

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾. Know that in it there are several benefits:

The first benefit: this surah is like a completion of the surahs before it, and like a foundation for the surahs after it. As for its being a completion of the surahs before it: Allah, exalted is He, made Surah al-Duha in praise of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and in detailing his circumstances. So at the beginning of that surah He mentioned three things relating to his prophethood:

The first is His words: ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested [you]﴾ [al-Duha: 3].

The second is His words: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾ [al-Duha: 4].

The third is: ﴿And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha: 5]. Then He concluded that surah by mentioning three of his circumstances, peace be upon him, concerning the worldly life, which are His words: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge? And He found you lost and guided [you]? And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient?﴾ [al-Duha: 6-8].

Then in Surah al-Sharh (Alam Nashrah) He mentioned that He honored him with three things:

The first: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1].

The second: ﴿And We removed from you your burden, which had weighed upon your back﴾ [al-Sharh: 2-3].

The third: ﴿And We raised for you your repute﴾ [al-Sharh: 4].

Then He honored him in Surah al-Tin with three kinds of honor:

The first: that He swore by his land, which is His words: ﴿And this secure city﴾ [al-Tin: 3].

The second: that He informed of the deliverance of his community from the Fire, which is His words: ﴿Except for those who believe﴾ [al-Tin: 6].

The third: their arrival at the reward, which is His words: ﴿For them is a reward uninterrupted﴾ [al-Tin: 6].

Then He honored him in Surah "Iqra'" with three kinds of honors:

The first: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1], meaning: recite the Qur'an rightly, seeking help through the name of your Lord.

The second: that He overcame his opponent by His words: ﴿Then let him call his associates; We will call the guards of Hell﴾ [al-'Alaq: 17-18].

The third: that He granted him the perfect nearness, which is: ﴿Prostrate and draw near﴾ [al-'Alaq: 19].

He honored him in Surah al-Qadr with the Night of Decree, which has three kinds of excellence:

The first: its being ﴿better than a thousand months﴾ [al-Qadr: 3].

The second: the descent of ﴿the angels and the Spirit therein﴾ [al-Qadr: 4].

The third: its being ﴿peace until the emergence of dawn﴾ [al-Qadr: 5].

He honored him in Surah Lam Yakun by honoring his community with three honors:

The first: that they are ﴿the best of creation﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 7].

The second: that ﴿their reward with their Lord is gardens﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 8].

The third: ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾.

He honored him in Surah "Idha Zulzilat" with three honors:

The first: His words: ﴿On that Day she will report her news﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 4], and this requires that the earth will testify on the Day of Resurrection for his community to their obedience and servitude.

The second: His words: ﴿On that Day people will depart separated to be shown their deeds﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 6], and this indicates that their acts of obedience will be displayed to them, so they will attain joy and happiness.

The third: His words: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7]. And the knowledge of Allah is without doubt greater than every great thing, so they must reach its reward.

Then He honored him in Surah al-'Adiyat by swearing by the horses of the warriors of his community, and He described those horses with three attributes: ﴿By the racing [horses], panting, and by those that strike sparks [of fire], and those that attack at dawn﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 1-3].

Then He honored his community in Surah al-Qari'ah with three matters:

The first: ﴿Then as for one whose scales are heavy﴾.

The second: that they are ﴿in a pleasant life﴾.

The third: that they will see their enemies in ﴿a blazing Fire﴾.

Then He honored him in Surah Alhakum (al-Takathur) by clarifying that those who turn away from his religion and law will become tormented in three ways:

The first: that they will see Hellfire.

The second: that they will see it with the certainty of sight.

The third: that they will be questioned about the bliss.

Then He honored his community in Surah al-'Asr with three matters:

The first: faith: ﴿except those who believe﴾ [al-Tin: 6].

The second: ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾.

The third: guiding creation to righteous deeds, which is enjoining one another to truth and enjoining one another to patience.

Then He honored him in Surah al-Humazah by mentioning that whoever slanders and defames, for him there are three kinds of punishment:

The first: that he will not benefit from his worldly wealth at all, which is His words: ﴿He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal﴾ ﴿No!﴾ [al-Humazah: 3-4].

The second: that he will be thrown into the Crushing Fire (al-Hutamah).

The third: that those doors will be closed upon him so that he will have no hope of exit, which is His words: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾ [al-Humazah: 8].

Then He honored him in Surah al-Fil by turning back the plot of his enemies upon their own necks in three ways:

The first: He made their plot go astray.

The second: He sent against them birds in flocks.

The third: (He made them like eaten straw).

Then He honored him in Surah Quraysh by taking care of the interests of his ancestors in three ways:

The first: He made them united and in agreement ﴿for the accord of Quraysh﴾.

The second: ﴿He fed them against hunger﴾.

The third: that He (granted them security against fear).

And He honored him in Surah al-Ma'un by describing those who deny his religion with three kinds of blameworthy attributes:

The first: baseness and meanness, which is His words: ﴿Who repulses the orphan﴾ ﴿and does not encourage the feeding of the poor﴾ [al-Ma'un: 2-3].

The second: abandoning the glorification of the Creator, which is His words: ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾ ﴿who make show﴾ [al-Ma'un: 5-6].

The third: abandoning benefit to creation, which is His words: ﴿and withhold [even] small kindnesses﴾ [al-Ma'un: 7].

Then, when He, glorified and exalted is He, had honored him in these surahs in these great ways, He said after them: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, meaning: Indeed, We have given you these abundant virtues mentioned in the preceding surahs, each one of which is greater than the entire kingdom of the world. So occupy yourself with worshipping this Lord, and with guiding His servants to what is most beneficial for them. As for worshipping the Lord, it is either with the self, which is His words: ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾, or with wealth, which is His words: (and sacrifice). As for guiding His servants to what is most beneficial for them in their religion and their worldly life, it is His words: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship"﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1-2]. Thus it is established that this surah is like a completion of the surahs before it. As for its being like a foundation for what comes after it: He, exalted is He, commands him after this surah to disavow all the people of the world by His words: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship"﴾, and it is well known that people's coercion regarding their creeds and religions is more severe than their coercion regarding their lives and wealth, because they expend their wealth and lives in defending their religions. Therefore, criticizing people's creeds stirs up enmity and anger more than any other criticism. When He commanded him to disavow all the people of the world and to refute their religions, it followed that all the people of the world would be in the utmost enmity toward him, and this is something from which every creature recoils, so one hardly dares to undertake it. Consider Musa, peace be upon him, how he feared Pharaoh and his army. Here, however, since Muhammad, peace be upon him, was sent to all the people of the world, every single creature was like Pharaoh in relation to him. So Allah, exalted is He, arranged, in removing this severe fear, a subtle arrangement, which is that He placed before that surah this surah. For His words: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ remove that fear from him in several ways:

The first: His words: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, meaning abundant good in this world and in religion, so this is a promise from Allah to him of support and protection, like His words: ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], and His words: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67], and His words: ﴿If you do not aid him, Allah has already aided him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40]. And whoever has Allah, exalted is He, as guarantor for his protection, does not fear anyone.

The second: when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, and this word encompasses the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter, and the good of this world had not yet reached him while he was in Mecca, and a breach of promise in the speech of Allah, exalted is He, is impossible, so it was required by the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, that He keep him alive in the abode of this world until those goods reach him. So that was like good tidings to him and a promise that they would not kill him, nor overpower him, nor would their plotting reach him, but rather his affair would increase in strength and power every day.

The third: when he, peace be upon him, declared them disbelievers, and discredited their religions, and called them to faith, they gathered around him and said: "If you do this seeking wealth, we will give you wealth until you become the richest of people; and if your aim is a wife, we will marry you to our most noble women; and if your aim is leadership, we will make you a leader over ourselves." Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, meaning: since the Creator of the heavens and the earth has given you the goods of this world and the Hereafter, do not be deceived by their wealth and their flattery.

Fourth: The verse "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar" indicates that Allah spoke with him directly, without an intermediary. This corresponds to His words: ﴿And Allah spoke to Moses directly﴾ [An-Nisa: 164]. Rather, this is more honourable, for when a master addresses his servant directly, with the commitment of nurture and kindness, that is higher than when he addresses him in other than this sense. It further produces strength in the heart and removes fear from the soul. Thus it is established that Allah's address to him with His words "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar" is among the things that remove fear from the heart and cowardice from the soul. Therefore He placed this surah before the surah "Say, O disbelievers" [Al-Kafirun: 1], so that he could be occupied with that arduous obligation and the undertaking of declaring the whole world to be disbelievers and displaying disassociation from their deities. It is as if He says: "When you obeyed My command, see how I fulfilled the promise to you and gave you a multitude of followers and supporters; indeed, the people of the world enter the religion of Allah in throngs." Then, when the matter of the call and the manifestation of the Sharia was complete, He began to explain what relates to the states of the heart and the inner self. This is because the seeker either has his seeking confined to this world, or he seeks the Hereafter. As for the seeker of this world, he has nothing but loss, humiliation and disgrace, and then his end is the Fire; this is what is meant by the surah "Perish the hands of Abu Lahab" [Al-Masad: 1]. As for the seeker of the Hereafter, the greatest of his states is that his soul becomes like a mirror in which the images of existing things are imprinted. It is established in the rational sciences that the way of creation in knowing the Creator is in two ways: among them are those who know the Creator and then, through knowing Him, reach knowledge of His creatures; this is the most noble and highest way. And among them are those who reverse this, and this is the way of the majority.

Then He, glorified be He, concluded His noble Book with that path which is the more noble of the two paths. He began with the mention of the attributes of Allah and the explanation of His majesty, which is the surah "Say, He is Allah, the One" [Al-Ikhlas: 1]. Then He followed it with the mention of the degrees of His creatures in the surah "Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak" [Al-Falaq: 1]. Then He concluded the matter with the mention of the degrees of the human soul, and at that point He ended the Book. This whole structure will only become clear in detail when this surah is explained in detail. So glory be to Him who guided the intellects to knowledge of these noble secrets deposited in His noble Book.

The second benefit in His words "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar" is that the word "Indeed (inna)" is sometimes intended to denote plurality, and sometimes intended to denote glorification.

As for the first: it indicates that the God is one, so it cannot be taken to mean plurality, except if it is intended that this gift is something that the angels, Gabriel, Michael and the earlier prophets strove to obtain, when Abraham asked for your sending, saying: ﴿Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 129], and Moses said: "My Lord, make me of the community of Ahmad." This is what is meant by His words: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Moses﴾ [Al-Qasas: 44], and the Messiah gave good tidings of you in His words: ﴿And a messenger giving good tidings of one who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [As-Saff: 6].

As for the second: that it is taken to mean glorification. In this there is an alert to the greatness of the gift, because the Giver is the Mighty One of the heavens and the earth, and the one to whom it is given is the one indicated by the particle of address in His words: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you﴾. The gift is the thing named al-Kawthar, and it indicates exaggeration in abundance. Since the word conveys the greatness of the Giver, of the one to whom it is given, and of the gift, how great is this blessing, how mighty and how sublime; and what an honour, how exalted it is.

The third benefit: a gift, though small, becomes great because it comes from a great giver. For this reason, when a great king throws an apple to one of his slaves as an act of honour, that is considered a great honour, not because the pleasure of the gift is in itself, but because its issuing from the great giver makes it great. Here, al-Kawthar, though in itself it is of the utmost abundance, increases in greatness and perfection because it issues from the King of creation.

The fourth benefit: when He said "We have granted you," He joined to it an indicator showing that He does not take it back. This is because, according to the school of Abu Hanifa, it is permissible for a stranger to take back his gift. But if the recipient takes a compensation, however small, it is not permissible for him to retract. For if a man gives a person something worth a thousand dinars, and then asks from him a comb worth a fils, and he gives it to him, the right of retraction is lost. So here, when He said "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar," He asked of him prayer and sacrifice, and the benefit of this is the cancellation of the right of retraction.

The fifth benefit: He built the verb upon the subject, and this indicates emphasis. The evidence for this is that when you mention the subject of which you speak, the intellect knows that you will inform about it with some matter, and so it remains eager to know what you will say about it. When you then mention that predicate, it accepts it as a lover accepts his beloved, and so this is more forceful in confirmation and in removing doubt and dispelling suspicion. From here you come to know the grandeur in His words: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded﴾ [Al-Hajj: 46], for it is more majestic than if He had said: "For indeed the eyes are not blinded." What confirms our statement is the saying of a great king to one who makes him a promise and guarantees him: "I will give you, I will suffice you, I will take charge of your affair." This is when the promised thing is a great matter about which leniency rarely occurs; its greatness gives rise to doubt about fulfilling it. But when it is ascribed to a great guarantor, that doubt then vanishes. This verse is of this kind, for al-Kawthar is a great thing about which leniency rarely occurs. So when

He put forward the subject, which is His words "Indeed (inna)," that attribution becomes one that removes that doubt and repels that suspicion.

The sixth benefit: He, the Exalted, opened the sentence with the particle of emphasis that functions in the manner of an oath, and the speech of the Truthful is preserved from breach. So how much more so when He has stressed the emphasis?

The seventh benefit: He said "We have granted you" and did not say "We will grant you," because His words "We have granted you" indicate that this granting was already accomplished in the past, and this contains several kinds of benefit:

The first: whoever has always been in the past honoured, cared for, and whose needs have been met, is more noble than one who will become so. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "I was a prophet while Adam was between water and clay."

The second: that it is an indication that God's judgment of felicity and wretchedness, of wealth and poverty, is not a matter that happens now, but was already in existence from eternity.

The third: it is as if He says: "We have already prepared the causes of your happiness before your entry into existence, so how would We neglect your affair after your existence and your occupation with worship?"

The fourth: it is as if He, the Exalted, says: "We did not choose you and did not prefer you on account of your obedience; otherwise We would have been obliged not to give you until after you had undertaken obedience. Rather We chose you purely by grace and kindness from Us towards you, without any cause compelling Us." This is an allusion to his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "He who accepted, accepted without a cause, and he who rejected, rejected without a cause."

* * *

The eighth benefit: He said "We have granted you," and did not say "We have granted the Messenger," or "the Prophet," or "the scholar," or "the obedient one," because if He had said that, it would indicate that that gift occurred as caused by that attribute. But when He said "We have granted you," it is known that that gift is not caused by any cause at all, but is pure choice and will, as He said: ﴿We have apportioned﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 32], and: ﴿Allah chooses messengers from the angels and from mankind﴾ [Al-Hajj: 75].

The ninth benefit: He first said: "Indeed We have granted you," then said secondly: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾. This indicates that His granting him guidance and success precedes our acts of obedience. And how could it not be so, when His giving to us is His attribute, and our obedience to Him is our attribute, and the attribute of the created does not affect the attribute of the Creator; rather, the one that has influence is the attribute of the Creator upon the attribute of the created. For this reason it is reported from al-Wasiti that he said: "I do not worship a Lord whom my obedience pleases and my disobedience angers." Its meaning is that His pleasure and His displeasure are eternal, while my obedience and my disobedience are temporal, and the temporal has no effect upon the eternal. Rather, His pleasure with the servant is what moved him to obedience in what never ceases; and likewise the matter of displeasure and disobedience.

The tenth benefit: He said "We have granted you al-Kawthar," and did not say "We have brought you (ātaynāka) al-Kawthar." The reason for this is two matters:

The first: that giving (ītāʾ) may be obligatory or may be bounty, whereas giving (iʿṭāʾ) is more akin to bounty. So His words "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar" mean: these abundant good things, namely Islam, the Qur'an, prophethood, and the fair remembrance in this world and the Hereafter, are pure bounty from Us to you, and there is nothing of it by way of entitlement or obligation. In this there is good news in two respects:

One of them: when the Generous One begins to nurture by way of bounty, the apparent meaning is that He does not nullify it; rather He increases it every day.

The second: that what is the cause of entitlement is measured by the measure of entitlement, and the deed of the servant is finite, so the entitlement obtained through it is finite. But bounty is the outcome of Allah's generosity, which is infinite, so His bounty is also infinite. Since His words "We have granted you" indicate that it is bounty and not entitlement, this indicates continuity and ever-increasing growth.

If it is said: Did He not say: ﴿seven of the oft-repeated and the Qur'an﴾ [Al-Hijr: 87]? We reply with two answers:

The first: that giving (iʿṭāʾ) entails possession, and possession is the cause of exclusive right. The proof of this is that when Solomon said: ﴿Grant me a kingdom﴾ [Sad: 35], He said: ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold without account﴾ [Sad: 39]. For this reason, whoever interprets al-Kawthar as the Basin says: "The community will be his guests." But giving (ītāʾ) does not entail possession, and for this reason He said regarding the Qur'an: "(We have brought you)" [Al-Hijr: 87], for it is not permissible for the Prophet to conceal any of it.

The second: that partnership in the Qur'an is partnership in knowledge, and there is no fault in that; but partnership in a river is partnership in material things, and that is a defect.

The second aspect, showing that giving (iʿṭāʾ) is more fitting to this station than bringing (ītāʾ), is that giving is used for the little and the much. God the Exalted said: ﴿and gave a little and then withheld﴾ [An-Najm: 34]. But bringing (ītāʾ) is used only for a great thing. God the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 252], and ﴿And We certainly gave David a bounty from Us﴾ [Saba: 10]. And ītiyy is the flowing torrent. Once this is established, His words "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar" indicate the magnifying of the station of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, in several respects:

One of them: meaning, this Basin is like a small, paltry thing in comparison with what is stored up for you of lofty ranks and noble degrees. So it contains good news of things greater than what is mentioned.

The second: that al-Kawthar is an allusion to water. It is as if He says: water in this world is below food; if the bounty of water is al-Kawthar, how then is the rest of the bounty?

The third: that the bounty of water is giving (iʿṭāʾ), and the bounty of Paradise is bringing (ītāʾ).

The fourth: it is as if He says: this which I have given you, though it is al-Kawthar, is in your regard a giving and not a bringing, because it is below your due. Customarily, when the giver is great, the gift, though great, is said to be small; that is, it is small in comparison with the greatness of the one to whom it is given. So it is here too.

The fifth: we may say that He said concerning what He gave him of al-Kawthar, "We have granted you (aʿṭaynāka)," because it is worldly, whereas the Qur'an is "bringing (ītāʾ)," because it is religion.

The sixth view: it is as if He is saying, "Everything you have received from Me is a gift, even if it is al-Kawthar (abundance). But the greatest part of that abundance is that you remain victorious and your enemy is cut off (abtar). We have given you this al-Kawthar in advance. As for the enduring remembrance and victory over the enemy, it is not fitting to bestow them except after an act of obedience from you that precedes them: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, that is, worship Me and ask Me for victory after the worship, for I have decreed by My generosity that after every obligatory act there is an answered supplication. This is what is related in the attributed (musnad) hadith. Then I will respond, and your enemy will become cut off (abtar), which is the one who is deprived of giving." This is what comes to mind in interpreting His words: ﴿Indeed, We have given you﴾.

As for al-Kawthar, in the language it is on the pattern fawal (a morphological form) from abundance (kathrah), and it denotes one who is excessive in abundance. It was said to a Bedouin woman whose son had returned from a journey, "With what has your son returned?" She said, "He returned with kawthar," meaning with a large number. It is also said of a man who is generous in giving, "He is a kawthar." Al-Kumayt said:

*"You are abundant, O son of Marwan, and good, and your father was the son of virtues, a kawthar."*

It is also said of dust when it rises and becomes thick: kawthar. This is the meaning of al-Kawthar in the language. The exegetes differed concerning it in several ways:

The first, which is the well-known and widely transmitted view among the early (salaf) and later (khalaf) scholars, is that it is a river in Paradise. Anas related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I saw a river in Paradise whose banks are domes of hollow pearls. I struck my hand into the course of the water, and behold, it was musk, very fragrant. I said, 'What is this?' It was said, 'It is al-Kawthar which Allah has given you.'" In the narration of Anas: "It is whiter than milk and sweeter than honey. In it are green birds with necks like the necks of Bactrian camels. Whoever eats from that bird and drinks from that water will attain Riḍwān (Allah's good pleasure)." Perhaps this river was named kawthar either because it is the most abundant of the rivers of Paradise in water and goodness, or because the rivers of Paradise gush forth from it, as it is related that there is no garden in Paradise except that it has in it a flowing river of al-Kawthar, or because of the great number of those who drink from it, or because of the abundance of benefits in it. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is a river which my Lord promised me, in which there is much good."

The second view: it is a basin (ḥawḍ), and the reports concerning it are well known. The way to reconcile this view with the first view is to say: perhaps the river flows into the basin, or perhaps the rivers flow from that basin, so that the basin is like the source.

The third view: al-Kawthar is his descendants. They said: this surah was only revealed in response to those who reproached him (ﷺ) for having no sons. So the meaning is that He will grant him offspring who will remain throughout the passage of time. Consider how many of the People of the House (Ahl al-Bayt) have been killed, yet the world is filled with them. And no one of consequence remains from the Banu Umayyah in the world. Then consider how many great scholars there were among them, such as al-Baqir, al-Sadiq, al-Kazim, al-Rida, peace be upon them, and al-Nafs al-Zakiyyah, and others like them.

The fourth view: al-Kawthar is the scholars of his community. By my life, this is indeed abundant good, for they are like the prophets of the Children of Israel. They love the remembrance of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they spread the traces of his religion and the signs of his law. The point of comparison is that the prophets agreed on the fundamentals of knowing Allah but differed in the law, as a mercy to creation, so that each person might reach what is good for him. Likewise, the scholars of his community all agree on the fundamentals of his law, but they differ on the branches of the law, as a mercy to creation. Then the excellence is in two respects:

The first: it is related that on the Day of Resurrection every prophet will be brought, followed by his community. Sometimes a messenger comes with one man or two men, while every scholar of his community is brought with many thousands. They gather before the Messenger, and sometimes the number of those who follow some scholars exceeds the number of those who follow a thousand prophets.

The second respect: they were correct because they followed the texts derived from revelation, and the scholars of this community are correct while exerting effort in deduction (istinbāṭ) and independent reasoning (ijtihād). Or, according to some, even if some of them err, the one who errs will also be rewarded.

The fifth view: al-Kawthar is prophethood. There is no doubt that it is abundant good, because it is the rank which is second to lordship (rubūbiyyah). For this reason He said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisā': 80]. It is half of faith. Rather, it is like the branch in the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, for the knowledge of prophethood must be preceded by knowledge of the essence of Allah, His knowledge, His power and His wisdom. Then, when the knowledge of prophethood is attained, from it are derived the knowledge of the rest of the attributes, such as hearing, sight, and the attributes of goodness and, according to some, the attributes of existence. Our Messenger received the greatest share of this excellence, for he is the one mentioned before all the other prophets and sent after them. Moreover, he was sent to both jinn and mankind (al-thaqalān), and he is the one who will be resurrected before all the prophets. It is not permissible for any law to abrogate his law (naskh). His virtues are more than can be counted or enumerated. Let us mention a few of them here, and so we say:

* * *

The book of Adam, peace be upon him, was words, as He said: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37]. The book of Ibrahim was also words, as He said: ﴿And when Allah tested Ibrahim with words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. The book of Musa was scrolls, as He said: ﴿The scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa﴾ [al-A'lā: 19]. As for the book of Muhammad (ﷺ), it is the book that is dominant (muhaymin) over all of them, as He said: ﴿And a guardian over it﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 48]. Also, Adam, peace be upon him, only challenged with scattered names, as He said: ﴿Tell Me the names of these﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], while Muhammad (ﷺ) challenged with arranged (poetic/organized) speech: ﴿Say: if mankind and the jinn gathered together﴾ [al-Isrā': 88].

As for Nuh, peace be upon him, Allah honored him by holding his ship upon the water. And He did to Muhammad (ﷺ) something greater than that. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) was on the bank of a body of water, and with him was ʿIkrimah ibn Abī Jahl. He said: "If you are truthful, call that stone which is on the other side, and let it swim and not sink." So the Messenger pointed to it, and the stone that he pointed to uprooted itself from its place, swam until it came before the Messenger, peace be upon him, greeted him, and bore witness to his prophethood. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Is this enough for you?" He said: "Not until it returns to its place." So the Prophet, peace be upon him, commanded it, and it returned to its place.

And He honored Ibrahim by making the fire cool and safe for him, and He did with regard to Muhammad (ﷺ) even greater than that. From Muhammad ibn Ḥāṭib, who said: "I was a child, and a cooking pot of fire spilled over me, and my whole skin was burned. My mother carried me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, 'This is the son of Ḥāṭib, who has been burned as you see.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spat upon my skin and wiped his hand over the burned part, and said: 'Remove the harm, Lord of mankind.' So I became healthy, with no harm in me."

And He honored Musa by splitting the sea for him on the earth, and He honored Muhammad by splitting the moon for him in the sky. Then consider the difference between the sky and the earth. He caused water to gush from the rock for him, and for Muhammad He caused water to gush from his fingers as springs. He honored Musa by having the cloud overshadow him, and likewise He honored Muhammad with this, for the cloud used to shade him. He honored Musa with the white hand, and He honored Muhammad with something greater than that, which is the Great Qur'an, whose light reached the East and the West. Allah turned the staff of Musa into a serpent. When Abu Jahl wanted to strike him with a stone, he saw two serpents on his shoulders, and he turned away in terror. The mountains glorified Allah along with Dawud, and the stones glorified Allah in his hand and in the hands of his companions. Whenever Dawud held iron, it became soft. When he (Muhammad) wiped a mangy sheep, it gave milk. He honored Dawud with birds gathered (to him), and Muhammad with the Buraq. He honored ʿIsā, peace be upon him, with the raising of the dead, and honored him with the like of that when the Jews hosted him with a poisoned sheep, and when he put the morsel in his mouth, it informed him. He healed the blind and the leper. It is related that the wife of Muʿādh ibn ʿAfrāʾ came to him, and she had leprosy, and she complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah wiped over her with a branch, and Allah removed the leprosy. And when a man's eyeball fell out on the day of Uhud, he picked it up and brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who returned it to its place. ʿIsā knew what people concealed in their houses, and the Messenger knew what his uncle had concealed with Umm al-Faḍl, so he informed him of it, and al-ʿAbbās accepted Islam because of that.

As for Sulayman, Allah returned the sun for him once. He did the same for the Messenger when he slept with his head in ʿAlī's lap, and woke up after the sun had set, so He returned the sun until he prayed. He returned it another time for ʿAlī, and he prayed ʿAṣr at its proper time. Allah taught Sulayman the language of the birds, and He did the same with regard to Muhammad. It is related that a bird had lost its young, so it began fluttering over his head and speaking to him. He said: "Who has bereaved this one of her young?" A man said: "I did." He said: "Return her young to her." And the speech of the wolf with him is well known. He honored Sulayman by his journey in a morning that lasted a month, and by letting him travel to Bayt al-Maqdis in an hour. His donkey Yaʿfūr used to be sent to whomever he wished and would bring him. People complained to him about a she-camel that had been made to nurse young (and was wild) and that they could not control it. He went to it, and when it saw him, it submitted to him. He sent Muʿādh to some regions, and when he reached the desert, behold, there was a lion crouching. That terrified him, and he did not dare to turn back. So he advanced and said: "I am the messenger of the Messenger of Allah," and it wagged its tail. Just as the jinn submitted to Sulayman, so they submitted to Muhammad, peace be upon him. When the Bedouin brought the lizard (ḍabb) and said: "I will not believe in you until this lizard believes in you," the lizard spoke, acknowledging his prophethood. When the gazelle, which the Bedouin had released, was given as a surety for him, it returned running until it brought him out of the pledge, and the trunk of the palm tree (ḥināyah) moaned at his separation from it. When the snake bit the heel of al-Ṣiddīq in the cave, it said: "I have been longing for him for so many years, so why have you kept me from him?"

He fed a great multitude from little food. His miracles are more than can be counted or enumerated. For this reason Allah placed him before those whom He chose, saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you and from Nuh﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 7]. Since his messengership was like this, it was permissible for Allah, the Exalted, to call it al-Kawthar, so He said: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾.

* * *

The sixth view: al-Kawthar is the Qur'an, and its virtues cannot be counted: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqmān: 27], ﴿Say: if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 109].

The seventh view: al-Kawthar is Islam. By my life, this is indeed abundant good, for through it the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter are attained, and through its loss the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter are lost. And how could it not be, when Islam is an expression for knowledge, or for what must include knowledge? He said: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. If Islam is abundant good, then it is al-Kawthar. If it is said: why did He specify it with Islam, when His blessings encompass all? We say: because Islam reached others from him, so he, peace be upon him, was like the origin of it.

The eighth view:

[Page 119]

The Kawthar is the great number of followers and supporters. There is no doubt that he has followers whom none but Allah can count. It is related that he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "I am the answer to the prayer of Allah's friend Abraham, I am the glad tidings of Jesus, and my intercession will be accepted on the Day of Resurrection. While I am with the prophets, a multitude of people will appear to us, and we will look at them eagerly. Every prophet hopes that they are his community. Then they appear with bright faces and limbs marked by the traces of ablution, and I say: 'My community, by the Lord of the Ka'bah!' They will enter Paradise without reckoning. Then something like what appeared at first will appear to us, and we will look at them eagerly, and every prophet hopes that they are his community. They appear with bright faces and limbs marked by the traces of ablution, and I say: 'My community, by the Lord of the Ka'bah!' They will enter Paradise without reckoning. Then three times as many as those raised before will be lifted up for us, and we will look at them eagerly." He mentioned it as he had mentioned it the first and second times, and then he said: "Three groups of my community will certainly enter Paradise before any other people." And he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "Marry, multiply, and increase in number, for I will boast of you before the nations on the Day of Resurrection, even with the miscarried child."

If he boasts of those who have not reached the age of legal responsibility, how much more of such a vast and great multitude? Therefore it was fitting for Him, exalted is He, to remind him of this great blessing, and so He said: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾.

The ninth opinion: al-Kawthar refers to the many virtues that are in him, for by the consensus of the community he is more excellent than all the prophets. Al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah said: one says "rajulun kawthar" when a man is generous and abounding in good. In Sihah al-Lughah, al-Kawthar is "the chief who is abundant in goodness." When Allah the Exalted granted Muhammad these great virtues, it was fitting for Him, exalted is He, to remind him of that great blessing, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾.

The tenth opinion: al-Kawthar is the elevation of remembrance, and its explanation has already passed in His words: ﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾.

The eleventh opinion: that it is knowledge. They said: interpreting al-Kawthar in this way is preferable, for several reasons:

First: knowledge is abundant good. He said: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know, and the grace of Allah upon you has been great﴾ [an-Nisa: 113]. He commanded him to seek knowledge, saying: ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]. He called wisdom "much good," saying: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269].

Second: we must either interpret al-Kawthar as the blessings of the Hereafter or as the blessings of this world. The first is not permissible, because He said "We have given" (a'taynaka), whereas the blessings of Paradise are what He will give, not what He has given. Therefore al-Kawthar must be interpreted as what reached him in this world. The most noble of the things reaching him in this world is knowledge, and prophethood is included within knowledge. So the word must be interpreted as knowledge.

Third: when He said ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, He followed it with ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾. Whatever precedes worship is knowledge (ma'rifah). This is why in Surat an-Nahl He said: ﴿That warn them that there is no deity except Me, so fear Me﴾ [an-Nahl: 2], and in Ta-Ha He said: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]. In both surahs He placed knowledge before worship. Moreover, the fa' of sequence (فاءُ التَّعْقِيبِ) in His words "fa-salli" (فَصَلِّ, "so pray") indicates that the giving of al-Kawthar is like the cause for this worship. It is known that what necessitates worship is nothing but knowledge.

The twelfth opinion: al-Kawthar is good character. They said: benefit from good character is general; the knowing and the ignorant, the animal and the rational all benefit from it. As for benefiting from knowledge, it is specific to rational beings. So the benefit of good character is more general, and therefore al-Kawthar must be interpreted as it. He, upon him be peace, was like this: to strangers he was like a father, untying their knots and fulfilling their needs. His good character reached the point that when they broke his tooth, he said: "O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know."

The thirteenth opinion: al-Kawthar is the praised station, which is intercession. In this world He said: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33], and in the Hereafter he said: "My intercession is for the people of major sins from my community." It is related from Abu Hurayrah that he, upon him be peace, said: "Every prophet has a prayer that is answered, and I have kept my prayer as an intercession for my community on the Day of Resurrection."

The fourteenth opinion: the intended meaning of al-Kawthar is this surah itself. He said: this is because, despite its brevity, it contains all the benefits of this world and the Hereafter, since it includes the miraculous from several aspects:

The first: if we interpret al-Kawthar as the abundance of followers, or as the abundance of offspring and the continuation of lineage, this is a report of the unseen, and it has occurred in agreement with it, so it is miraculous.

The second: He said ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, which points to the removal of poverty so that one is able to sacrifice. This has occurred, so this too is a report of the unseen.

The third: His saying ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾. The matter was as He reported, so it is miraculous.

The fourth: they were unable to oppose it despite its brevity. This establishes that the aspect of miraculousness lies in the perfection of the Qur'an. It is established through it, because when they were unable to oppose it despite its brevity, they would be even more unable to oppose the whole Qur'an. When the aspect of miraculousness has become manifest in it through these aspects, the prophethood is established. When prophethood is established, monotheism and the knowledge of the Creator are established, and religion and Islam are established, and it is established that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. When these matters are established, all the good of this world and the Hereafter is established. Thus this surah functions as a concise, strong, and comprehensive point establishing all the aims. It is small in form but great in meaning. Furthermore, it has a distinctive feature not found in others: it consists of three verses, and we have explained that each of them is miraculous. So it is miraculous by each of its verses and miraculous as a whole, and this feature is not found in the rest of the surahs. Therefore it may be that the intended meaning of al-Kawthar is this surah.

The fifteenth opinion: the intended meaning of al-Kawthar is all the blessings of Allah upon Muhammad, upon him be peace. This is what is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, because the word al-Kawthar encompasses a great abundance. There is no preference in interpreting the verse as some of these blessings over interpreting it as the rest, so it must be interpreted as all of them. It is related that when Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated this opinion from Ibn 'Abbas, some people said to him: "People claim that it is a river in Paradise." Sa'id said: "The river in Paradise is part of the abundant good that Allah has given him." Some scholars said: the apparent meaning of His words ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ requires that He has given him that al-Kawthar. Therefore the closest interpretation must be what Allah has granted him of prophethood, the Qur'an, the wise remembrance, and victory over enemies. As for the Pool and the rest of the reward prepared for him, although it may be said that it is included, since what is established by the decree of Allah's promise is like what has occurred, the truth is what we have presented first, because although these were prepared for him, it is not correct to say in the true sense that He had given him them at the time this surah was revealed in Makkah. It may be answered that one who acknowledges to his young child that he owns an estate may be said to have given him that estate, even though the child at that time is not fit to dispose of it. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 108, verse 2 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾. There are several issues concerning this verse.

**First issue: concerning His saying "So pray" (fa-salli, "pray"), there are several views.**

The first: the intended meaning is the command to pray. If it is asked: the fitting response to a blessing is gratitude, so why did He say "So pray" and not "So give thanks"?

The answer comes in several parts.

The first: gratitude is an expression of glorification, and it has three pillars.

One of them relates to the heart: that he knows the blessing comes from Him and not from anyone else.

The second relates to the tongue: that he praises Him.

The third relates to action: that he serves Him and shows humility before Him. Prayer includes these meanings and more than them. So the command to pray is a command to give thanks plus something additional, and therefore the command to pray is better.

The second: if He had said "So give thanks," that would suggest that he had not been grateful before. Rather, he had been, from the beginning of his affair, one who knew his Lord, obeyed Him, and was thankful for His blessings. As for prayer, he knew it only through revelation. He said: ﴿You did not know what the Scripture was, nor what faith was﴾ [al-Shura 42:52].

The third: when He first commanded him to pray, Muhammad (ﷺ) said: "How can I pray when I am not in a state of ablution?" Then Allah said: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾ [al-Kawthar 108:1]. Then Jibril struck the earth with his wing, and the water of al-Kawthar gushed forth, and he performed ablution. Then it was said to him at that moment: "So pray." However, if al-Kawthar is understood to mean prophethood, then it is as if He said: "I have granted you prophethood so that you may command yourself and all creation to acts of obedience, and the most noble of them is prayer. So pray to your Lord."

The second view: "So pray to your Lord" means "So give thanks to your Lord." This is the view of Mujahid and Ikrimah. According to this view, they mention several explanations for the function of the fa' in His saying "So pray":

The first: a warning that thanks for a blessing is obligatory immediately and not delayed.

The second: that the fa' of consequence here (fa' al-ta'qib) points to what was established in His saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:56]. Then He singled out Muhammad (ﷺ) in this matter with added emphasis, in His saying: ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr 15:99]. Also, He said to him: ﴿So when you are free, then labor﴾ [al-Sharh 94:7], meaning: "Then it is incumbent upon you to undertake another act right after the first." So how much more so after My blessing has reached you — should you not be obligated to begin giving thanks immediately after that?

The third view: "So pray" means "So supplicate to Allah," because prayer is supplication. The function of the fa' according to this interpretation is as if He, exalted is He, says: "Before your request and supplication, We did not withhold from you al-Kawthar; how then after your request? But: 'Ask and you will be given; intercede and your intercession will be accepted.' " This is because he was always concerned for his community.

Know that the first view is preferable, because it is closer to the usage of the Shari'ah.

**Second issue: concerning His saying ﴿to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, there are two views.**

The first, which is the view of the majority of exegetes: the intended meaning is the sacrifice of camels.

The second view: the intended meaning of His saying "and sacrifice" is an action connected with the prayer, whether before it, during it, or after it. Then they mention several explanations for this:

The first: al-Farra' said its meaning is "face the qibla."

The second: al-Asbagh ibn Nubata narrated from Ali (peace be upon him), who said: When this surah was revealed, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said to Jibril: "What is this sacrifice (nahirah) that my Lord has commanded me?" He said: "It is not a sacrifice, but He commands you that when you begin the prayer you raise your hands when you say the takbir, and when you bow, and when you raise your head from bowing, and when you prostrate. For this is our prayer and the prayer of the angels in the seven heavens, and every thing has an adornment, and the adornment of the prayer is raising the hands at every takbir."

The third: it has been narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he interpreted this sacrifice (nahr) as placing the two hands on the chest (nahr) during the prayer, and he said: "Raising the hands before the prayer is the habit of one seeking refuge and protection, and placing them on the chest is the habit of one who is humble and submissive."

The fourth: 'Ata' said its meaning is: sit between the two prostrations until your chest (nahr) becomes visible.

The fifth: it has been narrated from al-Dahhak and Sulayman al-Taymi that they said: "And sacrifice" means raise your hands after supplication up to your chest. Al-Wahidi said: The origin of all these views is from the nahr, which is the chest. The place where a camel is slaughtered is called the nahr, because its throat is in its chest, where the windpipe appears from the top of the chest. So the meaning of nahr in this context is hitting the nahr, just as one says "his head" or "his belly" when one strikes that part of him.

As for al-Farra's view that it is an expression for facing the qibla, Ibn al-A'rabi said: the nahr is a man standing in prayer opposite the mihrab, which means he sets his chest (nahr) opposite the qibla, and does not turn right or left. Al-Farra' said: "Their dwellings face one another (tatanahar)," meaning they face each other. And he recited:

*O Abu Hakam, are you not the paternal uncle of Mujalid,*
*and the lord of the people of al-Abtah, the one who faces (al-mutanahir)?*

The subtle meaning in this is as if He, exalted is He, says: "The Ka'bah is My House, and it is the qibla of your prayer and your heart, and the qibla of My mercy and the object of My care. So let the two qiblas face one another."

Most scholars said: It is better to take it as the sacrifice of camels, for several reasons:

The first: whenever Allah mentions prayer in His Book, He mentions zakat after it.

The second: the people used to pray and sacrifice to idols, so it was said to him: "So pray and sacrifice to your Lord."

The third: these acts are the etiquettes and parts of the prayer, so they would be included under His saying: ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾. Therefore it is necessary that the intended meaning of the sacrifice be something other than them, because it is unlikely that part of a thing would be joined by conjunction to the whole of it.

The fourth: His saying "So pray" points to the glorification of Allah's command, and His saying "and sacrifice" points to compassion for the creatures of Allah. The whole of servitude does not go beyond these two foundations.

The fifth: the use of the word nahr to mean sacrificing camels is more well known than its use in the other meanings mentioned. So the words of Allah must be understood according to it.

Having established this, we say: The Hanafis used this to argue for the obligation of the udhiyah (sacrifice on Eid al-Adha), saying: Allah commanded him to sacrifice, and he must have done it, because it is not permissible for him to abandon an obligation. And when the Prophet (peace be upon him) did it, it became obligatory upon us to do the same, based on His saying: ﴿and follow him﴾ [al-A'raf 7:158], and His saying: ﴿Follow me, and Allah will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:31]. Our companions (the Shafi'is) said: The command to follow is restricted by his saying: "Three things were written for me and not written for you: the Duha prayer, the Adha sacrifice, and the Witr prayer."

**Third issue: those who interpreted His saying "So pray" as the prayer have differed in several views.**

The first: that by prayer He meant the general category of prayer, because they used to pray to other than Allah and sacrifice to other than Allah. So He commanded him not to pray or sacrifice except to Allah, exalted is He. Those who permitted delaying the clarification of the general (mujmal, that which is unspecified) cited this verse as evidence, because He commanded prayer without explaining its manner. Abu Muslim answered and said: He meant by it the obligatory prayer, namely the five prayers, and the manner was not mentioned because the manner was already known beforehand.

The second view: He meant the Eid prayer and the udhiyah, because they used to put the udhiyah before the prayer, so this verse was revealed. The scholars who investigate said: This is a weak view, because the conjunction of one thing with another by the particle "and" (waw) does not necessitate order.

The third view: from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Pray the dawn prayer at Muzdalifah and sacrifice at Mina." The closer view is the first, because when the mention of sacrifice is joined with prayer, it is not necessary that the prayer be understood as what takes place on the Day of Sacrifice.

* * *

**Fourth issue: the lam in His saying ﴿to your Lord﴾ has several benefits.**

The first benefit: this lam (of devotion) relates to the prayer as the spirit relates to the body. Just as the body, from the crown of the head to the sole of the foot, is only good and praiseworthy if there is a spirit in it, but if it is dead it is only a thrown corpse, so too with prayer, bowing, and prostration: even if they are beautiful in form and long, if the lam of "to your Lord" is not in them, they are dead and thrown corpses. The meaning of His saying to Musa: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:14] is similar. It was also said: Their prayer and sacrifice used to be directed to an idol, so it was said to him: "Let your prayer and your sacrifice be for Allah."

The second benefit: it is as if He, exalted is He, says: In the earlier surah He mentioned that they used to pray for show. So you pray, not for show, but sincerely.

**Fifth issue: the fa' in His saying ﴿So pray﴾ indicates causation for two matters.**

The first: the causation of worship. It is as if it was said: "The abundance of My favor upon you makes it obligatory for you to occupy yourself with servitude."

The second: the causation of disregarding them. When they said to him: "You are cut off (abtar)," it was said to him: "Just as We have bestowed upon you these many blessings, occupy yourself with your obedience, and do not mind their saying and their nonsense."

Know that since abundant blessings are beloved, and what is necessarily connected to the beloved is also beloved, and the fa' in His saying "So pray" requires that prayer be one of the necessary consequences of those blessings, therefore prayer became the most beloved of things to the Prophet (peace be upon him). So he said: "The coolness of my eye has been placed in prayer." And he prayed until his feet swelled. It was said to him: "Has not Allah forgiven you what came before of your sin and what came after?" He said: "Should I not be a grateful servant?" His saying: "Should I not be a grateful servant?" is an indication that it is obligatory upon me to occupy myself with obedience, according to the requirement of the fa' in His saying "So pray."

**Sixth issue: Apparently, the more fitting phrasing would have been: "Indeed We have granted you al-Kawthar, so pray to Us and sacrifice." But He left this for His saying ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾, for several benefits:**

The first: that its coming in the manner of iltifat (a shift from the speaker to the addressed or from one grammatical person to another) is among the foremost of the doors of eloquence.

The second: that shifting speech from the pronoun to the explicit noun produces a kind of majesty and awe. From this is the saying of the caliphs to those they address: "The Commander of the Faithful commands you, and the Commander of the Faithful forbids you."

The third: His saying "Indeed We have granted you" does not explicitly state whether the speaker is Allah or someone else. Also, the word "Indeed we" (inna) can indicate plurality, just as it can indicate a single speaker who magnifies himself. So had He said "pray to Us," that possibility would have been eliminated — namely, that he did not know whether this prayer was for Allah alone or for Him and for others as a form of association. Therefore He left that wording and said: ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾, so that this possibility would be removed and monotheism in obedience and action would be stated explicitly for Allah, exalted is He.

**Seventh issue: His saying ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾ is more eloquent than His saying "So pray to Allah," because the word Lord (Rabb) indicates the earlier nurturing mentioned by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾, and it indicates a beautiful promise for the future: that He will continue to nurture him and will not leave him.**

**Eighth issue: there are two questions concerning the verse:**

The first: the thing mentioned after prayer is zakat, so why is what is mentioned here the sacrifice?

The second: why did He not say "Sacrifice" (dahhi) so that it would include all types of sacrifices?

The answer to the first: As for the view of the one who says the intended meaning of prayer is the Eid prayer, the matter is clear in it. As for the view of the one who understood it as prayer in general, there are several reasons:

The first: the polytheists' prayers and offerings were to idols, so it was said to him: "Make both of them for Allah."

The second: some people said that he (peace be upon him) did not own any of the goods of this world, but only possessed what was necessary. Therefore zakat was not obligatory upon him. As for the sacrifice, it was obligatory upon him, based on his saying: "Three things were written for me and not written for my community: the Duha prayer, the Adha sacrifice, and the Witr prayer."

Third: The most precious of wealth among the Arabs was camels, so He commanded him to sacrifice them and to devote them to the obedience of God, Exalted, as a reminder of severing the soul's attachments to the pleasures of this world and its good things. It is narrated that "he, peace be upon him, offered a hundred camels, among which was a male camel belonging to Abu Jahl with a gold ring in its nose. He, peace be upon him, sacrificed them himself until he grew tired, then he commanded 'Ali, peace be upon him, to do the rest. The she-camels were crowding around the Messenger of God, but when 'Ali took the knife, they moved away from him."

As for the answer regarding the second point: prayer is the greatest of the physical acts of worship, so He joined with it the greatest kind of sacrifice. Also, in it there is an indication that after your poverty you will reach a state where you slaughter a hundred camels.

Ninth issue: The verse indicates the obligation of performing the prayer before the sacrifice, not because the particle "wa" (and) necessitates sequence, but because of his saying, peace be upon him: "Begin with what God began with."

Tenth issue: The surah is Meccan according to the most sound opinions, and the command to sacrifice served as good news of the attainment of power and the removal of poverty and fear.

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off.﴾

Concerning this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The scholars have mentioned several views on the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*):

The first: "The Prophet, peace be upon him, used to leave the mosque while al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi was entering. They met and conversed. The chieftains of Quraysh were in the mosque. When he entered they said, 'Who was the one you were talking with?' He said, 'That cut-off one.'" I say: that was a private matter between some of them and others, yet God made it manifest, and so it would be a miracle. It is also narrated that al-'As ibn Wa'il used to say, "Muhammad is cut off (*abtar*), having no son to stand in his place after him; when he dies his mention will end and we will be rid of him." His son 'Abd Allah by Khadijah had died. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil, al-Kalbi, and the general body of the exegetes (*ahl al-tafsir*).

The second: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf came to Mecca, a group of Quraysh came to him and said, "We are the people of the water-supply and the keepers of the Ka'bah, and you are the lord of the people of Medina. Are we better, or this cut-off one from his people, who claims he is better than us?" He said, "Rather, you are better than him." Then there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾, and there was also revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, who believe in *jibt* and *taghut*?﴾ [al-Nisa': 51].

The third: 'Ikrimah and Shahr ibn Hawshab said: When God revealed to His Messenger and he called Quraysh to Islam, they said, "Muhammad has been cut off (*batara*)," meaning he has opposed us and separated from us. So God informed them that it is they who are cut off.

The fourth: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. When the son of the Messenger of God died, Abu Jahl said, "I hate him because he is cut off." This was foolishness on his part, for he hated him for a matter that was not in his choice, since the death of a son was not his (Muhammad's) intention.

The fifth: It was revealed concerning his uncle Abu Lahab, for when he confronted him with the words "Perish you!", he would say in his absence, "He is cut off."

The sixth: It was revealed concerning 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, and it was he who used to say that. Know that it is not unlikely that all those unbelievers said such things, for they used to say about him worse than that. Perhaps al-'As ibn Wa'il was the most persistent of them in this saying, and that is why the reports became famous that the verse was revealed concerning him.

* * *

**The second issue:** *Al-shana'* is hatred, and *al-sha'ini* is the one who hates. As for *al-batr*, linguistically it is the cutting off, severing. One says *batartuhu abtaruhu batran* and *buitara*, meaning he became *abtar*, that is, one whose tail is cut off. It is also said of one who has no offspring that he is *abtar*, and from this comes the *himar abtar*, the donkey with no tail. Likewise it is said of one from whom good has been cut off.

Then, when the unbelievers described him with this, God made clear that the one described by this attribute, in an exclusive sense, is that hater. For when you say "Zayd is the scholar", it implies that there is no scholar other than him. Knowing this, the unbelievers' description of him (peace be upon him) as *abtar* undoubtedly meant that good had been cut off from him—may God curse them.

Then this is either to be understood as a specific good or as all goods.

As for the first: it allows several views.

One: al-Suddi said: Quraysh used to say of anyone whose male children died that he was *butira* (cut off). When his son al-Qasim and 'Abd Allah died in Mecca, and Ibrahim in Medina, they said, "He has been cut off, having no one to stand in his place." Then God made clear that his enemy is the one described by this attribute, for we see that the progeny of those unbelievers has been cut off, while his progeny (peace be upon him) increases and grows every day, and so it will be until the Day of Resurrection.

Two: al-Hasan said: By calling him *abtar* they meant that he would be cut off from his aim before reaching it. God made clear that their opponent is the one who is like that, for they became retreating, defeated, and subdued, while the banners of Islam were raised high, and the peoples of East and West humbled themselves before it.

Three: They claimed he was *abtar* because he had no helper or supporter, but they lied, for God is his protector (*mawlah*), and Gabriel and the righteous believers are with him, while as for the unbelievers, they have no supporter or beloved left.

Four: *Al-abtar* is the lowly and humiliated. It is narrated that "Abu Jahl prepared a feast for a people, and then he described the Messenger of God with this description. Then he said, 'Stand up, let us go to Muhammad, wrestle him, and make him humble and lowly.' When they reached the house of Khadijah and agreed upon this, Khadijah brought out a mat. When they wrestled, Abu Jahl strove to throw him down, while the Prophet, peace be upon him, remained standing like a mountain. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) threw him in the most disgraceful manner. When he returned, he took him with his left hand, because the left hand is for cleansing after relieving oneself, so he was impure, and he threw him to the ground a second time and placed his foot upon his chest." Some storytellers (*qussas*) mentioned that the intended meaning of ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾ is this incident.

Five: When the unbelievers described him with this description, it was said: ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾, meaning: what they said about you is corrupt speech that will vanish and perish, whereas the praise we have mentioned of you remains for the duration of time.

Six: A man stood up before al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, peace be upon them both, and said, "You have blackened the faces of the believers by abandoning the leadership to Mu'awiyah." He said, "Do not harm me, may God have mercy on you. The Messenger of God saw in a dream the Banu Umayyah climbing his pulpit one by one, and that displeased him. So God revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾, and ﴿Indeed, We revealed it in the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. The rule of the Banu Umayyah was thus, then they were cut off and became cut off."

* * *

**The third issue:** When the unbelievers abused him, God answered on His own, without an intermediary, saying: ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾. Such is the custom of beloveds: when a beloved hears someone abusing his beloved, he himself takes up the reply. So here the Truth, glorified is He, undertook their answer. He did likewise in several places when they said: ﴿Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you that when you are completely torn apart you will be in a new creation?﴾ ﴿Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?﴾ [Saba': 7]. Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far error﴾ [Saba': 8]. When they said, "He is mad," He swore three times, then said: ﴿You are not, by the favour of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 2]. When they said: ﴿You are not a messenger﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43], He answered and said: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Qur'an, indeed you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 1–3]. When they said: ﴿Shall we leave our gods for a mad poet?﴾ [al-Saffat: 36], He refuted them and said: ﴿Rather, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat: 37], thus confirming him. Then He mentioned the threat to his adversaries and said: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾ [al-Saffat: 38]. When He related their words: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30], He said: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾ [Ya-Sin: 69]. When He related their saying: ﴿This is not but a fabrication he has invented, and others have helped him with it﴾ [al-Furqan: 4], He named them liars by His saying: ﴿They have come with injustice and falsehood﴾ [al-Furqan: 4]. When they said: ﴿What is with this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], He answered them and said: ﴿We did not send before you any messengers but that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]. How exalted is this honour!

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Know that when God gave him glad tidings of great blessings, and God knew that a blessing is not wholesome except when the enemy has been subdued, He therefore promised him the subduing of his enemy, saying: ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾. In this verse there are subtleties:

The first: It is as if God says: "I will not do this so that he may see some of the causes of your dominion, and some of the causes of his own affliction, so that rage will kill him."

The second: He described him as a hater (*sha'in*). It is as if God says: "This one who hates you has no power over anything except that he hates you. When the hater is unable to harm, his heart burns with rage and envy, and that enmity becomes among the greatest causes of affliction for that enemy."

The third: This order indicates that he became cut off only because he was a hater and an enemy of him. In truth it is so, for whoever opposes one who is envied has opposed God, Exalted is He, especially one whom He has undertaken to exalt and to magnify in rank.

The fourth: The enemy described Muhammad (peace be upon him) with paucity and humiliation, and himself with abundance and dominion, so God reversed the matter against him and said: "The mighty is whom God makes mighty, and the humiliated is whom God humiliates." So abundance and *al-kawthar* belong to Muhammad (peace be upon him), while cut-offness, baseness, and humiliation belong to the enemy. Thus between the beginning and end of the surah there arises a subtle kind of correspondence (*mutabaqah*).

* * *

**The fifth issue:** Know that whoever reflects on the openings and closings of this surah will realize that the benefits we have mentioned, in comparison with what God has kept to Himself of the benefits of this surah, are like a drop in the sea. It is narrated that Musaylimah opposed it and said: "Indeed We have given you the *jamahir*, so pray to your Lord and proclaim. Indeed your hater is a disbelieving man." The abandoned one did not realize that he himself is deprived of the sought-after goal, for several reasons:

First: The words and the arrangement are taken from this surah, and this does not constitute a true counterpart.

Second: We have said that this surah is like a completion of what precedes it and like a foundation for what follows it, so mentioning these words alone would neglect most of the subtleties of this surah.

Third: The great disparity which anyone with sound taste acknowledges between his saying ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾ and his saying "Indeed your hater is a disbelieving man." Among the subtleties of this surah is that each of the unbelievers described the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a different description: one described him as having no son, another as having no helper or supporter, and another as having no remembrance left of him. God, glorified is He, praised him with a praise that includes all virtues, namely His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾, for since He did not restrict that *kawthar* to any particular thing, it necessarily encompassed all the goods of this world and the Hereafter. Then He commanded him during his lifetime with the totality of acts of obedience, for acts of obedience are either acts of the body or acts of the heart. As for bodily obedience, its best forms are two: prayer, which is bodily obedience, and charity, which is obedience of wealth. As for obedience of the heart, it is that one does nothing except for the sake of God. The lam in His saying "for your Lord" (*li-rabbika*) indicates this state. Then it is as if He drew attention to the fact that obedience of the heart is not attained except after the attainment of bodily obedience, so He placed bodily obedience first in mention, namely His saying "pray" (*fa-salli*), and delayed the lam that indicates obedience of the heart, as an alert to the corruption of the doctrine of the people of *ibahah* (the permissivist sect), who hold that a servant may dispense with the obedience of his limbs through the obedience of his heart. This lam therefore indicates the falsity of the doctrine of *ibahah* and that sincerity (*ikhlas*) is indispensable. Then by the term "Lord" (*rabb*) He drew attention to the exaltedness of his state in the hereafter, as if He said: "I nurtured you before your existence; shall I abandon your nurturing after your persistence in these acts of obedience?" Then, just as He undertook at the beginning to pour out blessings upon him, He undertook at the end of the surah to defend him and to nullify the words of his enemies. This contains an indication that He, glorified is He, is the First in the outpouring of blessings and the Last in the perfecting of blessings in this world and the Hereafter. And God, glorified and exalted is He, knows best.
